reviewer: glm-5.3 (max effort) via glm-worker review mode
summary: Completed a read-only fact-check of all 48 files under the Computer Architecture course tree: root metadata, build script, EN/TH course metadata, 22 English lessons, and 22 Thai lessons. Audited all 88 checkpoints; EN/TH checkpoint IDs and correct-answer arrays match. Found one wrong/ambiguous answer key, several overgeneralized architecture and OS claims, standards-date issues, portability gaps, and limited Thai drift. No files were changed.

findings.message: throughput-vs-latency.json cp-2, "What will adding more worker threads achieve?", marks C ("Little — each request still takes as long") but B is at least equally correct and is the better general answer. Adding workers can reduce observed response latency when requests are queued by serving more requests concurrently; it has little effect only when queueing is absent or cores are already saturated. Reword the scenario to exclude queueing or key B.

The cheatsheet states, "Reduced architectures offer four modes: register, immediate, base plus offset, PC-relative," but the lesson itself says aarch64 is RISC and has scaled-index and pre-index modes. The nearby claim "Architectures with complex instruction sets have all of those, and more" is also not true for every CISC ISA. Scope this to base RISC-V and avoid universal claims about all reduced or complex architectures.

"A leaf function calls nothing, so nothing will overwrite its return address, so there is nothing to save — and therefore no frame" is an invalid universal claim. A leaf can require a frame for spilled values, address-taken locals, variable-length arrays, outgoing stack arguments, or ABI-required stack alignment. Say that the particular trivial leaf needs no frame.

"Branches and jumps encode an offset from the current instruction rather than an absolute address" is too broad. RISC-V conditional branches and JAL are PC-relative, but JALR targets a register plus immediate and is used for indirect branches, returns, and many far calls. Restrict the statement to branch/JAL encoding and note that full position independence can still involve GOT/PLT or other relocations.

The table row "DDR4 | 2014" is false if "Introduced" means standards introduction: JEDEC published JESD79-4 in September 2012. 2014 better describes broader commercial availability. Either date the standard publication correctly or label the column as widespread availability.

hit-miss-and-write-policy.json cp-1 keys B, "Write-allocate fetches each block before writing into it, while writing a complete line lets the hardware skip that fetch," as though universal. Full-line behavior is implementation-dependent: conventional write-allocate caches may still fill, while store buffers, write-validate/no-fetch-allocate, non-temporal stores, or write combining can avoid or hide the fill. State the assumed cache policy and present the measured result as implementation-specific.

bandwidth-numa-hbm.json cp-3 keys "Placed every physical page on the initialising thread's node," but Linux/NUMA placement is policy- and configuration-dependent. First-touch placement is common under the default local allocation policy, but memory bindings, transparent huge pages, migration, auto-NUMA balancing, and allocation flags can change the outcome. Replace "every" with the behavior under a stated default first-touch policy.

The lab step "Take any four-byte word from a real binary and decode it with your program" followed by "Compare your answer with objdump on the same address" is not runnable as written for most learners: no RISC-V binary is supplied, a host binary will not decode as RISC-V, and the default host objdump may lack RISC-V support. Provide a known word/binary and the exact cross-platform objdump invocation or prerequisite toolchain installation.

Thai equivalence drift: the Thai paragraph omits the English sentence "and a pre-index mode that updates the base register." Consequently, Thai learners lose the explicit aarch64 exception that qualifies the lesson's RISC-V-only addressing-mode discussion. Add the missing pre-index example to the corresponding Thai paragraph.

The DDR5 text says "to 8800 in the current standard" and identifies JESD79-5C from April 2024. JEDEC's later catalog lists JESD79-5D in November 2025, so the word "current" is stale as of 2026. Keep the dated JESD79-5C example but avoid claiming it is the current revision.

"A backtrace is a walk over saved return addresses; overflow attacks target the same field" overgeneralizes debugger behavior. Frame-pointer backtraces are only one mechanism; when frame pointers are omitted, debuggers commonly use DWARF CFI/e unwinder metadata or platform unwind records. Clarify the frame-chain case and mention unwind metadata.

The step "If your machine has multiple sockets or NUMA nodes, check with: numactl --hardware" is not portable as written. numactl is a separate Linux package and absent on macOS and many minimal Linux/WSL setups. Provide no-tool Linux alternatives such as lscpu plus /sys NUMA topology, and state the required package when recommending numactl.

Thai calling-convention cp-1 explanation is malformed: "และไม่สร้างเลยให้ตัวที่ไม่มี frame มีอยู่เพราะการเรียก" does not parse coherently and obscures the intended relation between calls and frames. Rewrite it to state that the compiler emits a full frame for a function containing a call and no frame for the call-free example.

The caption "Measured on an Apple M4" and the associated custom performance numbers are UNVERIFIED from the repository alone; analogous benchmark claims occur in other lessons. Verification requires the benchmark source, compiler/version and flags, OS/version, core/power configuration, repetition methodology, variance, and machine-reported cache/memory topology. The course appropriately tells learners to reproduce measurements on their own hardware.
